sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Event Sourcing is a persistence pattern where every state-changing operation is appended as an immutable, ordered event to a durable log, the log is the source of truth, and current state is derived by replaying events — with snapshots and projections added for performance and read scalability.

Event Sourcing inverts the usual persistence model. A traditional CRUD service stores current state: when a customer's address changes, the row in `customers` is overwritten, and the previous value is lost. An event-sourced service instead appends an `AddressChanged` event to an append-only log, and the current address is computed by replaying the log. The log is the source of truth; the current-state row (if it exists at all) is a derived projection. This shift sounds small but has outsized consequences for audit, temporal queries, bug recovery, and integration. Banks have operated this way for centuries — a checking account is an ordered ledger of deposits and withdrawals, and the balance is the sum of the ledger. Modern event-sourced systems generalize the ledger to any domain aggregate: an order, a shopping cart, a user session, a billing account.

The canonical architecture has four parts. The **event store** is an append-only log keyed by aggregate ID, ordered by sequence number; events are immutable, so the only write operation is `append(aggregate_id, event, expected_version)`. The **aggregate** is the domain object whose state is reconstructed by replaying its events through a `apply(event)` method; mutations go through a `handle(command)` method that validates invariants and emits new events. The **snapshot store** caches the aggregate's state every N events, so a 10-year-old account with 100k events can be rebuilt from the latest snapshot plus a few hundred events instead of the full log. The **projection** is a read-optimized view (a denormalized table, a search index, a materialized view) rebuilt by a consumer that subscribes to the event stream and updates the view as events arrive. The projection decouples the write model (events, normalized, write-optimized) from the read model (denormalized, query-optimized), which is the foundation of CQRS — Topic 11. Real-world deployments include Netflix's billing system (every charge, refund, and credit is an event; the current balance is a projection), Walmart's inventory (every stock movement is an event; the on-hand count is a projection), and Microsoft's e-commerce platform (orders, carts, and user profiles are event-sourced).

The compelling benefits are audit, temporal queries, and bug recovery. **Audit**: because every state change is an immutable event with a timestamp and causation ID, you can answer "who changed what when, and why" without an auxiliary audit log — the event log *is* the audit log. Financial regulators require exactly this kind of append-only history, which is why event sourcing is the default in fintech (Stripe, Square, Adyen). **Temporal queries**: you can reconstruct the state of any aggregate at any past time by replaying the event log up to that time — "what was the customer's address when this invoice was issued on March 14?" is a query an event-sourced system answers natively, while a CRUD system cannot answer it at all (the old address was overwritten). **Bug recovery**: when a bug in the projection logic is found and fixed, you replay the entire event log through the fixed projection, rebuilding the read model correctly without losing data — a fix that would require a multi-week data migration in a CRUD system. Netflix used exactly this pattern when they discovered a billing bug in 2018: the fix was a one-line code change and a 4-hour projection rebuild, with zero data loss and zero downtime.

The trade-offs are real and must be faced honestly. First, **complexity**: event sourcing adds an event store, a snapshot store, a projection mechanism, and a schema-evolution story — a 3-table CRUD service becomes 6 components. Second, **eventual consistency on reads**: the projection lags behind the write by the consumer's processing time (typically milliseconds, but visible to users in race conditions like "I just placed an order but the orders page does not show it"). Third, **schema evolution**: events are immutable, but the domain model changes — an `AddressChanged` event in 2020 with `city` and `state` fields may need to handle a 2024 migration to `city`, `state`, and `country`. The standard fix is event versioning (`AddressChanged.v1`, `AddressChanged.v2`) with upcasters that transform old events to new events on read. Fourth, **snapshot invalidation**: when the aggregate's `apply` logic changes (a bug fix), all snapshots are stale and must be rebuilt — the standard mitigation is to version the snapshot schema and rebuild on version mismatch. Fifth, **deletes are hard**: GDPR's right-to-be-forgotten requires deleting a user's data, but events are immutable — the standard patterns are cryptographic shredding (delete the encryption key for that user's events) or tombstoning (mark the user deleted and filter them from all projections).

The architect's rule is to use event sourcing when audit, temporal queries, or complex domain logic justify the complexity, and to avoid it for simple CRUD where the audit log is unused. The canonical anti-pattern is event-sourcing a user-profile table that changes once a quarter — the audit log is unused, the projection lag is a nuisance, and the team pays the complexity cost for no benefit. The canonical pro-pattern is event-sourcing a billing account that requires regulatory audit, supports dispute resolution (replay the events to show the customer exactly what happened), and feeds downstream analytics (the same events power both the operational system and the data warehouse). Stripe, Square, and Adyen all event-source their billing systems for exactly these reasons; the cost is a team of engineers maintaining the event store, and the benefit is a regulatory-grade audit trail and a single source of truth that powers both operations and analytics.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD C[Client Command
e.g. ChangeAddress] AGG[Aggregate: Customer
replays events -> state] ES[(Event Store
append-only log)] SNAP[(Snapshot Store
every N events)] PROJ1[Projection: Customers table] PROJ2[Projection: Search index] PROJ3[Projection: Analytics DW] C -->|handle cmd, validate| AGG AGG -->|append events, expected_version| ES ES -->|"on rebuild: replay from snapshot"| AGG SNAP --> AGG AGG -->|save snapshot every 100 events| SNAP ES -->|subscribe to event stream| PROJ1 ES --> PROJ2 ES --> PROJ3 PROJ1 --> R1[Read API] PROJ2 --> R2[Search API] PROJ3 --> R3[BI Dashboard] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +---------+ handle(ChangeAddress cmd) +-------------------+ | Client |------------------------------------>| Aggregate: cust_42| +---------+ +---------+---------+ | replay events | | to rebuild state | +---------+---------+ | append(events, expected_v) | v +--------------------------------------------------------------+ | Event Store (append-only log keyed by aggregate_id) | | cust_42: [Created, AddressSet(LA), AddrChanged(SF), ...] | +-----+-----------------+-----------------+-------------------+ | | | rebuild on demand | subscribe | subscribe | | | v v v +-----------------+ +---------------+ +---------------+ | Snapshot Store | | Projection: | | Projection: | | cust_42 @ v97 | | customers_tbl | | search_index | +-----------------+ +-------+-------+ +-------+-------+ | | v v Read API Search API append-only log IS the audit log; projections are derived, rebuildable ``` ### Walkthrough 1. A client sends a `ChangeAddress` command to the aggregate. The aggregate loads its current state — either by replaying events from the event store or by loading the latest snapshot and replaying only events after the snapshot's version — and validates the command against invariants. 2. If the command is valid, the aggregate emits an `AddressChanged` event (or several), appends it to the event store with the expected version (optimistic concurrency: the append fails if another writer advanced the version), and updates its in-memory state by applying the event. 3. A projection consumer subscribed to the event stream picks up the new event and updates the read-optimized view (e.g., the `customers` table). Snapshots are periodically saved (every N events) so future rebuilds start from the snapshot instead of the full log.

quiz.explanation: Snapshots cache the aggregate's state every N events so that rebuilding a 10-year-old aggregate with 100k events can start from the latest snapshot plus a few hundred events instead of replaying the entire log. Without snapshots, rebuild time grows linearly with event count, and an account opened in 2015 takes seconds to load — unacceptable for an interactive API.

An event is a fact that has already happened — "AddressChanged(new=SF)" — and cannot be rejected because it is in the past. The aggregate receives a command, validates it against current state, and if valid emits one or more events to the log.
